Why This Is Asked

Key Concepts

```
  default_memory: "128Mi"
```

```
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: pod-resource-defaults
webhooks:
  - name: default-resources.example.com
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: policy-webhook
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical handling of in-cluster secret management, file-watching, and safe API exposure.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes Secrets and RBAC
- InitContainers and sidecars
- In-cluster API calls with kubectl
- NetworkPolicy scoping and TLS rotation

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-rotator
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secret-rotator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secret-rotator
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: secrets
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: secrets-pvc
      containers:
        - name: rotator
          image: example/secret-rotator:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /secrets
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: rotator-creds
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache kubectl jq"]
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: reg-creds
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotence of secret refresh?
- What RBAC policies would you apply to limit permissions?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a safe, observable canary rollout using standard Kubernetes resources and NGINX Ingress without a service mesh.

## Key Concepts
- Canary deployment pattern with separate Deployments
- Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary, canary-weight)
- Progressive traffic shifting and rollback strategy
- Observability: latency, error rate, saturation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Stable Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: stable
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: stable
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Canary Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend-canary
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:1.2-canary
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Ingress (production path)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: frontend-ingress
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    # enable canary routing for the canary backend
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: "frontend.example.com"
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: frontend-canary
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you promote canary to 50% and then 100% safely?
- What metrics would you monitor to decide progression or rollback?
- How would you rollback if the canary fails without affecting stable users?

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD candidates must diagnose real issues with limited tools. This tests debugging flow, resource tuning, and readiness/liveness strategies.

## Key Concepts
- OOMKilled diagnosis through pod events and logs
- Resource requests/limits tuning and safety margins
- Probes (readiness and liveness) to recover from bad states

## Code Example
````yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myrepo/web-app:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "1Gi"
            cpu: "1000m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
````

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate changes in a staging environment before production?
- What trade-offs exist between higher requests/limits and cluster density?

## Why This Is Asked

- PVC-backed logs

- Cleanup Job for namespace teardown

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: test-plan
data:
  plan.yaml: |
    steps:
      - name: ping
        url: http://target-service:8080/health
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: harness-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  endpoint: aHR0cDovL3NhbXBsZS5jb20vcmVzdGFydA==
```

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: testbench
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-curl
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl || true"]
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      containers:
      - name: tester
        image: curlimages/curl:8.0

        volumeMounts:

```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests partitioned StatefulSet upgrades, PDB, and probes in a real CKAD scenario.

## Key Concepts
- StatefulSet partitioned RollingUpdate
- PodDisruptionBudget for minimum availability
- readinessProbe and startupProbe usage
- Resource requests/limits in containers

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
  namespace: prod
spec:
  serviceName: "cache"
  replicas: 3
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: cache
        image: myrepo/cache:2.0
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "300m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["bash","-lc","redis-cli PING"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        startupProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["bash","-lc","true"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 30
```

```javascript
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: cache-pdb
  namespace: prod
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
```

- How would you monitor for anomalies during the upgrade?

## Why This Is Asked
Assesses ability to combine CronJobs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and NetworkPolicy to automate in-namespace validation and remediation with idempotent patching and durable logs.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob, InitContainer, ConfigMap, Secret
- In-cluster scripting with kubectl/jq
- API-driven remediation and PVC-based logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy RBAC considerations

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton (CronJob with remediation Job)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ns-test-runner
spec:
  schedule: '0 * * * *'
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache kubectl jq"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          containers:
            - name: runner
              image: bitnami/kubectl:1.28
              command: ["sh", "-c", "bash /scripts/run.sh"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
                - name: policy
                  mountPath: /policy
                - name: secret
                  mountPath: /secret
              readinessProbe:
                httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
              livenessProbe:
                httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: ns-logs-pvc
            - name: policy
              configMap:
                name: ns-test-policy
            - name: secret
              secret:
                secretName: compliance-api-token
```

- Trade-offs: drift risk from patches, RBAC scope, log retention, and complexity of in-namespace remediation.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical Kubernetes operational skills including StatefulSet storage migration, configuration change propagation, health monitoring, security hardening, and availability guarantees during disruptions.

## Key Concepts
- PersistentVolumeClaim integration with StatefulSets and StorageClass selection
- ConfigMap checksum annotations for automated rolling updates
- Health probe configuration (readiness vs liveness)
- Pod security context with non-root execution and file system permissions
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintaining service availability
- Load testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Strategic merge patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/collector
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/collector
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: collector-config
          items:
          - key: config
            path: config
        annotations:
          checksum/config: "{{ .Values.configChecksum }}"
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: "fast-ssd"
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Verification Strategy
Monitor rollout progress: `kubectl rollout status statefulset/collector -n telemetry`
Validate pod health: `kubectl get pods -n telemetry -l app=collector -w`
Check PVC binding: `kubectl get pvc -n telemetry`
Load test using k6 or hey targeting collector endpoints
Verify ConfigMap changes trigger restarts by updating ConfigMap and watching pod recreation

## Rollback Approach
Use `kubectl rollout undo statefulset/collector -n telemetry` for immediate rollback
For complex issues, restore from previous StatefulSet manifest and scale down/up
Always validate PDB compliance during rollback to avoid availability violations

```javascript
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: heartbeat-cron
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:

          initContainers:
          - name: install-deps
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl"]
          containers:
          - name: heartbeater
            image: alpine:3.19

            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: cron-config
            - secretRef:
                name: target-creds
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
```

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates practical Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) skills across multiple resource types and patterns in a realistic production scenario. It tests the ability to compose distributed system components while understanding security boundaries.

## Key Concepts Tested

1. **ConfigMap/Secret Integration**: Properly referencing ConfigMap values and Secret data as environment variables to configure the application.

2. **InitContainer Pattern**: Performing one-time setup tasks—like installing tools—before the main application container starts.

3. **Sidecar Containers**: Running auxiliary containers alongside the main application for cross-cutting concerns like TLS certificate management.

4. **Health Probes**: Configuring readiness and liveness probes to manage pod traffic and restart behavior.

5. **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting network egress to enforce least-privilege access between namespaces and services.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Forgetting to mount ConfigMap/Secret values into the container environment
- Not handling signal propagation in infinite loops (leading to graceful shutdown issues)
- Overly restrictive NetworkPolicies that block necessary egress routes
- Misconfiguring probe thresholds that cause premature restarts or delayed traffic routing

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD wiring: PVC usage, InitContainer tooling, manifest validation, per-namespace health aggregation, internal POST, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for tooling setup and pre-flight checks
- PVC mounting and runtime manifest processing
- Sidecar for TLS rotation
- Probes for reliability
- Secrets for credentials
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: health-agg
  namespace: ckad
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: health-agg
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: health-agg
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: manifests
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: svc-manifests-pvc
        - name: tls
          secret:
            secretName: tls-secret
      initContainers:
        - name: prep
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq curl && kubeval /svc-manifests/*.yaml || true"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /svc-manifests
      containers:
        - name: health-agg
          image: myorg/health-agg:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /svc-manifests
        - name: tls-sidecar
          image: myorg/tls-sidecar:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls
              mountPath: /tls
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test startup under load and verify network isolation across namespaces?
- What changes would you make to support dynamic manifest updates without pod restart?
